title: Kripa's counsel in the dark
hookLine: an old teacher is shaken awake in the dark and told the plan, and he tries to talk his nephew out of it
carry: fate and effort work together; ask the elders

cards: Kripa opens his eyes. It's still dark. His nephew is standing over him, and so is Kritavarma, who's been woken too.
Ashvatthama tells them what he saw in the tree and what he means to do: go to the Pandava camp tonight, while everyone sleeps, and kill the men who killed his father. Kripa is old.
He taught the princes on both sides when they were boys, and he has fought this whole war beside Duryodhana. Now, half awake under a banyan, he has a few minutes to change his nephew's mind.

teach.b: Kripa doesn't shout. In Ganguli's telling he starts with a teaching Hindu thinkers return to again and again: daiva and purushakara, what fate gives and what a person does. Success needs both together.
Effort alone isn't enough, and neither is fate. Then he gets practical. Don't decide this alone, he says, in effect.
Let's go to Dhritarashtra, to Gandhari, to the wise Vidura, and ask them what should be done. And he names the thing directly: killing men who are asleep is not honored in this world.
Ashvatthama has an answer for everything.
The Panchalas broke the rules first, he says. Dhrishtadyumna killed my father while he sat with his weapons laid down.
He cannot sleep while they live, and he doesn't care if he's reborn as a worm or an insect for it.
Then he yokes his horses, and Kripa and Kritavarma, who argued against him, follow. So here's the teaching under the banyan. Hindus don't believe in sitting back and calling it fate; effort matters.

But effort has to be joined to the right time and to wise counsel. That's why Hindu families take big decisions to their elders, and ask a blessing before they begin. Kripa offered exactly that, and it was refused.
When you're sure you have to act right now, Kripa's counsel is the old one: do the work, but not alone, and not before you've asked the people who love you.

how: Kripa's counsel under the banyan, with its talk of fate and human effort working together, is a passage some readers return to when they think about fate and action in the Mahabharata.

o: the night book, where good counsel loses in the dark
the teacher's plea to strike the camp while it sleeps
the council of elders Ashvatthama goes to consult

games.q: the argument at night — tap the pairs.

s: Kripa urged Ashvatthama to strike while the camp slept
he urged him to ask the elders first and said killing sleepers is not honored.
Kripa said success needs both fate and effort
daiva and purushakara: he taught that neither alone is enough.
Kripa went home after Ashvatthama refused his advice
he and Kritavarma followed Ashvatthama toward the camp.

games.q: you're Ashvatthama. Kripa has just said fate and effort must work together, and that the elders should be asked first. what would his counsel have you do?
o: drive to the camp tonight; effort is all that counts.
go to Dhritarashtra, Gandhari and Vidura before acting.
do nothing; whatever happens is fate.
games.why: that was Kripa's counsel: effort joined to wise counsel. Ashvatthama refused it and yoked his horses.

practice: Before something big begins, many Hindus bow to their elders and ask for a blessing, ashirvad. Bring to mind a decision you're carrying.
Picture the elder or friend whose counsel you trust, and picture telling them plainly what you mean to do. Breathing in, hear what they might say. Breathing out, decide to ask them for real.
If you pray, you can ask God's blessing on the decision too.

wordCard.voice: Sauptika. The night book, where an old teacher names fate and effort, begs his nephew to ask the elders first, and is refused.

orig.note: Kripa: teacher of the princes and Ashvatthama's uncle, who counsels him under the banyan.

carryVoice: Your line: fate and effort work together; ask the elders. Kripa was right, and followed anyway. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Mahabharata, Sauptika Parva, Kripa's counsel on fate and effort, his advice to consult Dhritarashtra, Gandhari and Vidura, and Ashvatthama's reply
